excerpt: How whiplash compensation is calculated in Georgia and South Carolina — injury grades, medical bills, lost wages, and what shared fault does to a claim.
keyTakeaways: Whiplash injuries range from Grade 0 (no symptoms) to Grade IV (fractures or dislocations), and compensation covers medical bills, lost wages, pain and suffering, and diminished quality of life. Georgia's modified comparative fault rule (O.C.G.A. SS 51-12-33) bars recovery at 50% or more fault, while South Carolina bars recovery at 51% or more. Filing deadlines are two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. SS 9-3-33) and three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code SS 15-3-530). Thorough medical documentation and consistent treatment records are critical to maximizing a whiplash claim.

faqs.question: How much is a whiplash injury claim worth?
faqs.answer: The value of a whiplash claim depends on the severity of your injury, the duration of your recovery, your medical expenses, and your lost income. Mild whiplash that resolves within weeks may result in settlements of $2,500 to $10,000, while severe whiplash with chronic symptoms can be worth $50,000 to $150,000 or more. An experienced attorney can evaluate the specific facts of your case and provide a realistic estimate.

faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a whiplash injury claim in Georgia and South Carolina?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, you have 2 years from the date of injury to file a personal injury lawsuit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). In South Carolina, the deadline is 3 years from the date of injury (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Missing these deadlines means losing the right to pursue compensation entirely, so it is important to consult an attorney as soon as possible after your accident.

faqs.question: Can I still recover compensation if I was partially at fault for the accident?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. Georgia follows a modified comparative fault rule that allows you to recover damages as long as you are less than 50% at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). South Carolina allows recovery if you are less than 51% at fault. In both states, your compensation is reduced by your percentage of fault. For example, if you are 20% at fault and your damages total $50,000, you would receive $40,000.

faqs.question: Why are my whiplash symptoms delayed after the accident?
faqs.answer: It is very common for whiplash symptoms to appear days or even weeks after an accident. The adrenaline and stress hormones released during a collision can mask pain signals, and inflammation in the soft tissues of the neck may take time to develop fully. This is why medical professionals recommend seeking an evaluation immediately after any accident, even if you feel fine at the scene.

faqs.question: What evidence do I need to prove a whiplash injury claim?
faqs.answer: Key evidence includes medical records documenting your diagnosis, treatment plan, and the progression of your symptoms; photographs of the accident scene and vehicle damage; the police report; a personal pain journal describing your daily symptoms and limitations; records of all medical expenses and lost wages; and witness statements. The stronger your documentation, the more difficult it becomes for the insurance company to undervalue your claim.

faqs.question: Should I accept the insurance company's first settlement offer for my whiplash injury?
faqs.answer: In most cases, no. Initial settlement offers from insurance companies are almost always lower than the true value of a whiplash claim. Insurers make early offers hoping you will accept before you fully understand the extent of your injury and future treatment needs. An attorney can review any offer, calculate the full value of your damages including future medical costs, and negotiate for a fair settlement on your behalf.
